title: Behold a Prehistoric Lizard Tail Trapped in Amber - Nautilus
gist: A fingertip-sized (18 mm) piece of amber dated to 98.8 million years ago contains a shed lizard tail, showing tail autotomy as a predator-evasion tactic dates to at least the Late Cretaceous. The specimen has been held at Israel's Steinhardt Museum of Natural History since 2022 and was newly described in a study.

insights.claim: A lizard tail trapped in amber dated to 98.8 million years ago shows that lizards have used tail-shedding to escape predators since at least the Late Cretaceous.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Long-lived survival strategies illustrate the evolutionary durability of simple, effective defenses.
insights.quote: researchers have found a discarded tail in a block of amber that dates back 98.8 million years, to the time of the Late Cretaceous when dinosaurs roamed the Earth.

insights.claim: Many modern lizards detach their tails when grabbed by predators; the shed tail keeps wriggling as a distraction while the lizard escapes and later regrows a replacement.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Tail regeneration remains a reference biological model for regenerative research.

insights.claim: The amber specimen containing the lizard tail measures just 18 millimeters across, roughly fingertip size.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Small amber inclusions continue to yield significant paleontological findings.
insights.quote: The piece of amber analyzed by researchers measures just 18 millimeters (0.7 inches) across, so we’re talking fingertip size.

insights.claim: The lizard-tail amber has been held at the Steinhardt Museum of Natural History in Israel since 2022 but was only described in a newly published study.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Museum collections hold undescribed specimens, with a multi-year lag before scientific publication.

insights.claim: The amber find supports the principle that an escape trick that works tends to persist: lizards have kept the same evasion tactic for almost 100 million years.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Evolutionary stability of proven strategies is a useful analogy for durable competitive defenses.
insights.quote: If you’ve got an escape trick that works, stick with it
